kurals.tamil:
பருகுவார் போலினும் பண்பிலார் கேண்மை
பெருகலிற் குன்றல் இனிது.
kurals.transliteration:
Parukuvaar poalinum panpilaar kenmai
perukalir kundral inidhu.
kurals.meaning: Even when people of poor character seem so fond of you that they could drink you in, it is sweeter for that friendship to shrink than to grow.
kurals.elementary: Some people hug you so tightly and say so many nice things that it feels wonderful. But if they are not kind or honest underneath, it is better to let that friendship get smaller instead of bigger, just like you would slowly back away from a puppy that wags its tail and also bites.
kurals.university: The chapter on tee natpu (தீ நட்பு, ‘evil friendship’) opens with its sharpest image: parukuvaar (பருகுவார்), ‘those who would drink you up’, describing a show of affection so intense it seems to swallow the friend whole. The defect is panpu-ilaar (பண்பிலார்), ‘those without good character’, so the warmth is not the test; character is. Mu. Varadarasanar and Solomon Pappaiah both stress that the excess is appearance (‘தோன்றினாலும்’, ‘நடிக்கும்’), and Kalaignar speaks of being drowned in a flood of affection; all agree the right course is kundral (குன்றல்), letting the bond dwindle, rather than an abrupt break. This sets the chapter’s practical tone: Valluvar is less interested in condemning bad friends than in teaching how to reduce their hold. The text is identical in ytamizh and thirukkural.net; the sandhi-joined edition at thirukkural-thamizh.org prints ‘குன்ற லினிது’, a difference of word division only.

hinduism.quote_or_event: In the Hitopadesha’s first book, a jackal makes friends with a deer, flattering him and staying close, because he hopes to eat the deer’s flesh; he leads the deer into a farmer’s snare, and only the deer’s old friend, a crow, saves him.
hinduism.explanation: The jackal’s friendship is all warmth on the surface and appetite underneath, and the deer nearly dies of it.
hinduism.tie_back: This is the Kural’s ‘friend who would drink you up’ made literal: affection masking a wish to consume.
hinduism.source: Hitopadesha, Book I (Mitralabha), the deer, the crow and the jackal
hinduism._accuracy_note: Strong thematic match; summarised from the traditional story, not quoted.

christianity.quote_or_event: “He that hateth dissembleth with his lips, and layeth up deceit within him; When he speaketh fair, believe him not: for there are seven abominations in his heart.”
christianity.explanation: Proverbs warns that pleasant speech can be a cover for hostility, so fair words alone should not win trust.
christianity.tie_back: Like the Kural, it tells the reader to judge by the heart, not by the show of warmth.
christianity._accuracy_note: Close on the deceptive show; Proverbs speaks of open hatred hidden, the Kural of shallow character.

islam.quote_or_event: “And of the people is he whose speech pleases you in worldly life, and he calls Allah to witness as to what is in his heart, yet he is the fiercest of opponents.”
islam.explanation: The verse describes a person whose words charm and who swears to his sincerity, yet who is in fact a bitter adversary.
islam.tie_back: Both texts warn that pleasing, affectionate speech can hide a character that works against you.
islam._accuracy_note: Strong match on charming words over bad character; the verse concerns an adversary rather than a friend.

judaism.quote_or_event: Absalom, plotting against his father King David, would take the hand of anyone who came to bow before him and kiss him, and so, the narrator says, he stole the hearts of the men of Israel.
judaism.explanation: Absalom’s overflowing affection was a political tool in service of a rebellion, not a sign of good character.
judaism.tie_back: It shows exactly the Kural’s danger: lavish closeness from someone whose character does not deserve trust.
judaism._accuracy_note: Good narrative illustration; it concerns a rebel courting the public rather than a personal friendship.

buddhism.quote_or_event: “The friend who appropriates, the friend who renders lip-service, the friend that flatters, the friend who brings ruin, these four as enemies the wise behold, avoid them from afar as paths of peril.”
buddhism.explanation: The Buddha tells the young Sigala that some who look like friends are really foes and should be kept at a distance.
buddhism.tie_back: The Kural likewise refuses to let the appearance of friendship decide the matter and counsels reducing contact.
buddhism._accuracy_note: Same counsel of distance from false friends; the Sutta urges avoidance outright, the Kural a gradual waning.

greek_mythology.quote_or_event: “How handsome is the Crow,” he exclaimed, “in the beauty of her shape and in the fairness of her complexion!”
greek_mythology.explanation: In Aesop’s fable the Fox praises the Crow lavishly only to make her open her beak and drop the meat he wants.
greek_mythology.tie_back: The Fox’s gushing praise is the Kural’s ‘as though they would drink you up’: warmth that serves an appetite.
greek_mythology.source: Aesop, The Fox and the Crow (tr. G. F. Townsend)
greek_mythology._accuracy_note: Flattery rather than friendship; captures the false warmth but not the idea of a bond to be reduced.

philosophy.quote_or_event: “for the flatterer is a friend in an inferior position, or pretends to be such and to love more than he is loved”
philosophy.explanation: Aristotle notes that the flatterer performs a love greater than he receives, and that most people enjoy this because they want to be loved.
philosophy.tie_back: The Kural’s friend of poor character likewise wins us by an excess of displayed love, which is exactly why it must be watched.
philosophy.source: Aristotle, Nicomachean Ethics VIII.8 (tr. W. D. Ross)
philosophy._accuracy_note: Good on performed excess of love; Aristotle analyses rather than prescribes withdrawal.

kurals.tamil:
உறின்நட்டு அறினொருஉம் ஒப்பிலார் கேண்மை
பெறினும் இழப்பினும் என்.
kurals.transliteration:
Urinnattu arinoruum oppilaar kenmai
perinum izhappinum en.
kurals.meaning: Unworthy people make friends when there is something to gain and leave when the gain is gone; whether you win or lose such friendship makes no difference.
kurals.elementary: Imagine a classmate who sits with you only on days you bring cookies, and walks away when you don’t. Having that ‘friend’ or not having them is really the same, because they were only ever friends with the cookies.
kurals.university: The couplet is built on two paired verbs: urin nattu (உறின் நட்டு), ‘when there is gain, befriending’, and arin oruum (அறின் ஒரூஉம்), ‘when it ends, departing’; ar- here means ‘to cease or be cut off’, and oruu is the lengthened (alapedai) form of ‘leave’. The subjects are oppilaar (ஒப்பிலார்), which Mu. Varadarasanar and Puliyur Kesigan take as ‘the unworthy’ or ‘those of unequal nature’, while Solomon Pappaiah reads it with a twist, ‘those who have no equal in doing this’. The closing ‘en’ (என், ‘what of it?’) is a rhetorical shrug: such friendship is neither gain nor loss. Texts differ in spelling the second word: ytamizh has ‘அறினொருஉம்’, thirukkural.net prints ‘அறின்ஙருஉம்’ (apparently a typographic slip), and the sandhi-joined edition gives ‘உறினட் டறின்னொரூஉ’; the meaning is unaffected.

hinduism.quote_or_event: “He who loses his money is forsaken by his friends, his wife, his servants and his relations; yet when he regains his riches those who have forsaken him come back to him.”
hinduism.explanation: Chanakya observes, with some cynicism, that many relationships simply follow wealth, leaving when it goes and returning when it comes back.
hinduism.tie_back: This is precisely the Kural’s friend who comes with gain and leaves with loss.
hinduism.source: Chanakya Niti 15.5 (Sri Chanakya Niti-sastra, English translation)
hinduism._accuracy_note: Near-direct match; Chanakya draws a cynical conclusion about wealth that the Kural does not.

christianity.quote_or_event: “Wealth maketh many friends; but the poor is separated from his neighbour.”
christianity.explanation: Proverbs notes that prosperity attracts friends and poverty drives them off.
christianity.tie_back: Both describe friendship that tracks advantage, which is why the Kural says losing it costs nothing.
christianity._accuracy_note: Clear match on the observation; Proverbs states the fact without the Kural’s verdict on its worthlessness.

islam.quote_or_event: “And of the people is he who worships Allah on an edge. If he is touched by good, he is reassured by it; but if he is struck by trial, he turns on his face [to the other direction].”
islam.explanation: The verse describes loyalty that holds only while things go well and turns away at the first trial.
islam.tie_back: The same fair-weather pattern the Kural sees in unworthy friends: present in gain, gone in loss.
islam._accuracy_note: Analogous pattern, but the verse concerns faith in God, not human friendship.

judaism.quote_or_event: “All love that depends on a something, [when the] thing ceases, [the] love ceases; and [all love] that does not depend on anything, will never cease.”
judaism.explanation: The Mishnah distinguishes love tied to some benefit, which ends when the benefit ends, from love that depends on nothing and lasts, citing David and Jonathan as the lasting kind.
judaism.tie_back: This is the Kural’s gain-based friendship exactly, and it explains why its loss is no loss.
judaism._accuracy_note: Very close structural match: conditional love ends with its condition.

buddhism.quote_or_event: “One is a bottle friend; one says, ‘friend, friend’ only to one’s face; one is a friend and an associate only when it is advantageous.”
buddhism.explanation: In the Sigalovada Sutta the Buddha lists kinds of hollow companions, including the one who is a friend only when it pays.
buddhism.tie_back: This is the Kural’s urin nattu, arin oruum: friend while there is advantage, gone when there is none.
buddhism._accuracy_note: Near one-to-one match on the advantage-only friend.

greek_mythology.quote_or_event: “He who shares the danger ought to share the prize.”
greek_mythology.explanation: In Aesop’s fable of the Two Travelers and the Axe, one man says ‘I have found an axe’, not ‘we’, but when the owner gives chase he cries ‘we are undone’; his companion tells him to keep saying ‘I’.
greek_mythology.tie_back: The finder wants partnership only in loss, the mirror image of the Kural’s friend who wants it only in gain; both are the same selfish calculation.
greek_mythology.source: Aesop, The Two Travelers and the Axe (tr. G. F. Townsend)
greek_mythology._accuracy_note: Same theme of partnership shaped by self-interest, seen from the reverse side.

philosophy.quote_or_event: Seneca tells Lucilius that a friendship entered for one’s own advantage is a bargain, and that the man who begins to be your friend because it pays will also stop being your friend because it pays.
philosophy.explanation: For Seneca, friendship made for profit carries its own ending inside it, because the reason for it can disappear.
philosophy.tie_back: Valluvar draws the same conclusion: since such friendship comes and goes with gain, having it or losing it is all one.
philosophy.source: Seneca, Moral Letters to Lucilius, Letter 9
philosophy._accuracy_note: Very close in thought; paraphrased because the wording could not be checked against a live text.

kurals.tamil:
உறுவது சீர்தூக்கும் நட்பும் பெறுவது
கொள்வாரும் கள்வரும் நேர்.
kurals.transliteration:
Uruvadhu seerthookkum natpum peruvadhu
kolvaarum kalvarum ner.
kurals.meaning: The friend who weighs up what he stands to get, the one who loves only for the fee, and the thief are all the same kind of person.
kurals.elementary: If someone is your friend only after checking what they can get from you, they are a bit like a person who takes things without asking. A real friend doesn’t keep a price list.
kurals.university: Valluvar sets three figures in a row and declares them ner (நேர், ‘equal’): the friend who does seerthookkal (சீர்தூக்கல், ‘weighing on a balance’) of uruvadhu (உறுவது, ‘what will come to him’); those who take only peruvadhu (பெறுவது, ‘what they receive’); and kalvar (கள்வர், ‘thieves’). The middle phrase, peruvadhu kolvaar, is read by Mu. Varadarasanar, Puliyur Kesigan and Kalaignar, following the traditional gloss, as women who sell their company for payment; Solomon Pappaiah renders it as sex workers. The point is not to single anyone out but to define calculating friendship as a transaction for gain and to class it with taking what is not freely given. All three web texts agree on the wording; the sandhi-joined edition writes ‘சீர்தூக்கு நட்பும்’ and ‘கள்வரு நேர்’, a matter of spelling convention.

hinduism.quote_or_event: “The prostitute has to forsake a man who has no money, the subject a king that cannot defend him, the birds a tree that bears no fruit, and the guests a house after they have finished their meals.”
hinduism.explanation: Chanakya lists relationships that last only as long as there is something to take from them.
hinduism.tie_back: The list even begins with the same figure as the Kural, and makes the same point: such attachment is calculation, not friendship.
hinduism.source: Chanakya Niti 2.17 (Sri Chanakya Niti-sastra, English translation)
hinduism._accuracy_note: Striking parallel in imagery and logic; Chanakya describes rather than condemns.

christianity.quote_or_event: “This he said, not that he cared for the poor; but because he was a thief, and had the bag, and bare what was put therein.”
christianity.explanation: John explains that Judas objected to an act of generosity not out of concern for the poor but because he kept the common purse and stole from it.
christianity.tie_back: A disciple who measured everything by what he could take is the Kural’s gain-weighing friend, and John, like Valluvar, calls him a thief.
christianity._accuracy_note: Vivid parallel of a calculating companion labelled a thief, though it is a single narrative case.

islam.quote_or_event: “And among them are some who criticize you concerning the [distribution of] charities. If they are given from them, they approve; but if they are not given from them, at once they become angry.”
islam.explanation: The verse describes people whose approval of the Prophet rose and fell with what they personally received.
islam.tie_back: Their goodwill is the Kural’s seerthookkum natpu, friendship weighed against personal gain.
islam._accuracy_note: Good match on loyalty measured by reward; the setting is communal charity, not private friendship.

judaism.quote_or_event: “Many will intreat the favour of the prince: and every man is a friend to him that giveth gifts.”
judaism.explanation: This proverb in the Hebrew Bible observes that friendliness flows toward whoever has something to give.
judaism.tie_back: Friendship that follows gifts is the calculated kind the Kural classes with taking for gain.
judaism._accuracy_note: Same observation; the proverb is descriptive and lacks the Kural’s comparison to thieves.

buddhism.quote_or_event: “(i) he appropriates his friend’s wealth, (ii) he gives little and asks much, (iii) he does his duty out of fear, (iv) he associates for his own advantage.”
buddhism.explanation: The Buddha describes the ‘appropriator’, a foe disguised as a friend whose companionship is a way of taking.
buddhism.tie_back: Valluvar’s gain-weighing friend and the Buddha’s appropriator are the same person, and both texts treat him as a taker rather than a friend.
buddhism._accuracy_note: Very close match, item for item.

greek_mythology.quote_or_event: In Euripides’ Hecuba, King Priam sends his youngest son Polydorus, with a store of gold, to his guest-friend Polymestor of Thrace for safekeeping; when Troy falls, Polymestor murders the boy and keeps the gold.
greek_mythology.explanation: A sworn bond of guest-friendship is weighed against profit, and profit wins.
greek_mythology.tie_back: Polymestor is the Kural’s calculating friend who turns out to be no better than a thief.

philosophy.quote_or_event: “Now those who love each other for their utility do not love each other for themselves but in virtue of some good which they get from each other.”
philosophy.explanation: Aristotle defines friendship of utility as love directed not at the person but at the benefit.
philosophy.tie_back: This is the analytical version of the Kural’s friend who weighs what he will gain.
philosophy.source: Aristotle, Nicomachean Ethics VIII.3 (tr. W. D. Ross)
philosophy._accuracy_note: Precise conceptual match; Aristotle is less harsh, allowing utility friendships a lesser legitimacy.

kurals.tamil:
அமரகத்து ஆற்றறுக்கும் கல்லாமா அன்னார்
தமரின் தனிமை தலை.
kurals.transliteration:
Amarakaththu aatrarukkum kallaamaa annaar
thamarin thanimai thalai.
kurals.meaning: Better to be alone than to have as companions people who are like an untrained horse that throws its rider in the middle of battle.
kurals.elementary: If you ride a bike with wobbly brakes, it might fail just when you’re going downhill. A friend who leaves you at the scariest moment is like that bike, and it’s safer to walk on your own.
kurals.university: The image is martial: amarakam (அமரகம்) is ‘the battlefield’, kallaa maa (கல்லா மா) ‘a horse that has not been trained’, and aatrarukkum (ஆற்றறுக்கும்) describes it cutting the rider off midway, whether by throwing him (Mu. Varadarasanar, Kalaignar) or bolting from the field (Puliyur Kesigan, who widens maa to ‘an untaught beast’). Thamar (தமர்) means ‘one’s own people, intimates’, and the verdict is thanimai thalai (தனிமை தலை): solitude is supreme. The couplet sharpens the chapter’s logic: a bad friend is not merely useless but dangerous at exactly the moment you depend on him. The texts agree; the sandhi-joined edition writes ‘அமரகத் தாற்றறுக்குங் கல்லாமா வன்னார் தமரிற் றனிமை தலை’.

hinduism.quote_or_event: “It is better to be without a kingdom than to rule over a petty one; better to be without a friend than to befriend a rascal”
hinduism.explanation: Chanakya ranks having no friend above having a bad one, in a series of ‘better without’ comparisons.
hinduism.tie_back: This is the Kural’s thanimai thalai, solitude over unworthy company, stated almost word for word.
hinduism.source: Chanakya Niti 6.13 (Sri Chanakya Niti-sastra, English translation)
hinduism._accuracy_note: Near-direct match on the verdict; lacks the battlefield image.

christianity.quote_or_event: “Confidence in an unfaithful man in time of trouble is like a broken tooth, and a foot out of joint.”
christianity.explanation: Proverbs compares trusting an unfaithful person in a crisis to leaning on a body part that gives way under load.
christianity.tie_back: Like the untrained horse in battle, the unfaithful man fails exactly when you put your weight on him.
christianity._accuracy_note: Very close image of failure under pressure; lacks the preference for solitude.

islam.quote_or_event: “But when the two armies sighted each other, he turned on his heels and said, ‘Indeed, I am disassociated from you.’”
islam.explanation: The verse describes Satan encouraging the Quraysh before Badr and promising to protect them, then abandoning them as battle was joined.
islam.tie_back: A protector who vanishes when the armies meet is the Kural’s horse that throws its rider on the battlefield.
islam._accuracy_note: Remarkably close battlefield desertion image; the subject is Satan, not a human friend.

judaism.quote_or_event: “Nittai the Arbelite used to say: keep a distance from an evil neighbor, do not become attached to the wicked, and do not abandon faith in [divine] retribution.”
judaism.explanation: The Mishnah advises keeping one’s distance from bad neighbours and not attaching oneself to the wicked.
judaism.tie_back: Both teach that distance, even isolation, is better than attachment to people who will fail or harm you.
judaism._accuracy_note: Same counsel of distance; no image of desertion in crisis.

buddhism.quote_or_event: “If for company you cannot find a wise and prudent friend who leads a good life, then, like a king who leaves behind a conquered kingdom, or like a lone elephant in the elephant forest, you should go your way alone.”
buddhism.explanation: The Dhammapada advises walking alone rather than settling for unworthy companions.
buddhism.tie_back: This is the Kural’s thanimai thalai in Buddhist form: solitude over bad company.
buddhism._accuracy_note: Strong match on choosing solitude; no desertion image.

greek_mythology.quote_or_event: “Never travel with a friend who deserts you at the approach of danger.”
greek_mythology.explanation: In Aesop’s fable, one traveler climbs a tree and leaves his companion to face a bear alone; the survivor says the bear ‘whispered’ this advice to him.
greek_mythology.tie_back: The deserting friend is the untrained horse of the Kural, and the moral is the same: better to go alone.
greek_mythology.source: Aesop, The Bear and the Two Travelers (tr. G. F. Townsend)
greek_mythology._accuracy_note: Near one-to-one match on desertion in danger.

philosophy.quote_or_event: Seneca urges Lucilius to withdraw into himself as far as he can and to associate only with people who will make him better, since bad company infects the character.
philosophy.explanation: For Seneca, keeping one’s own company is preferable to company that weakens or corrupts.
philosophy.tie_back: It shares the Kural’s preference for solitude over unreliable companions, though on moral rather than practical grounds.
philosophy.source: Seneca, Moral Letters to Lucilius, Letter 7
philosophy._accuracy_note: Next-best match; Seneca worries about moral contagion, not desertion in crisis; paraphrased.

kurals.tamil:
செய்தேமஞ் சாராச் சிறியவர் புன்கேண்மை
எய்தலின் எய்தாமை நன்று.
kurals.transliteration:
Seydhemanj saaraach chiriyavar punkenmai
eydhalin eydhaamai nandru.
kurals.meaning: The shabby friendship of small-minded people, who will not stand by you as protection even when you have done everything for them, is better never gained than gained.
kurals.elementary: Think of an umbrella with holes in it. You can carry it, take care of it and open it every time, but it still won’t keep you dry. Some friends are like that, and it’s better not to count on them at all.
kurals.university: The key compound is seydhemam saaraa (செய்தேமம் சாரா): ēmam (ஏமம்) is ‘protection, safety’, and the phrase means ‘not coming to be a protection even when it has been made one’. Mu. Varadarasanar reads it as ‘though set to guard, they do not guard’, Solomon Pappaiah as ‘though we help them in many ways, they are no protection to us’, and Puliyur Kesigan as ‘they do not come to rescue us when trouble arrives’. Chiriyavar (சிறியவர்) are ‘the small’, people mean in mind, and their bond is pun-kenmai (புன்கேண்மை), ‘paltry friendship’. The conclusion, eydhalin eydhaamai nandru, ‘not attaining is better than attaining’, extends 814: such friendship is not neutral but a net loss. The text is uniform across the three sources, the sandhi-joined edition writing ‘யெய்தலி னெய்தாமை’.

hinduism.quote_or_event: “He is a true friend who does not forsake us in time of need, misfortune, famine, or war, in a king’s court, or at the crematorium (smasana).”
hinduism.explanation: Chanakya defines a true friend by presence in hardship, listing the moments when friends are most needed.
hinduism.tie_back: The Kural’s petty friends are the negative of this definition: they fail to be a protection when it counts.
hinduism.source: Chanakya Niti 1.12 (Sri Chanakya Niti-sastra, English translation)
hinduism._accuracy_note: Inverse statement of the same test; does not say such friends are better avoided.

christianity.quote_or_event: “At my first answer no man stood with me, but all men forsook me: I pray God that it may not be laid to their charge.”
christianity.explanation: Paul recalls that at his first defence before the court, none of his companions stood by him.
christianity.tie_back: It is the experience the Kural warns of: companions who are no protection in the hour of need.
christianity._accuracy_note: Matches the failure of protection; Paul forgives rather than concluding such friends are better not had.

islam.quote_or_event: “Oh, woe to me! I wish I had not taken that one as a friend.”
islam.explanation: On the Day of Judgement the wrongdoer regrets the companion who led him astray.
islam.tie_back: This is the Kural’s eydhalin eydhaamai nandru voiced as regret: better never to have had that friend.
islam._accuracy_note: Shares the ‘better never to have befriended’ verdict, but the harm is spiritual misguidance, not failure to protect.

judaism.quote_or_event: “To him that is afflicted pity should be shewed from his friend … My brethren have dealt deceitfully as a brook, and as the stream of brooks they pass away”
judaism.explanation: Job complains that his friends, like seasonal streams, ran dry just when he needed them.
judaism.tie_back: Job’s friends are the Kural’s pun-kenmai: no protection when it matters.
judaism._accuracy_note: Good image of failed support; Job does not conclude friendship is better avoided.

buddhism.quote_or_event: “(i) he guards the heedless, (ii) he protects the wealth of the heedless, (iii) he becomes a refuge when you are in danger, (iv) when there are commitments he provides you with double the supply needed.”
buddhism.explanation: The Buddha describes the true ‘helpmate’ friend as one who protects and becomes a refuge in danger.
buddhism.tie_back: The Kural’s petty friends are the exact opposite: they never become the refuge (ēmam) a friend should be.
buddhism._accuracy_note: Inverse match; the ‘refuge in danger’ phrase mirrors ēmam closely.

greek_mythology.quote_or_event: When Philoctetes was bitten by a snake on the way to Troy and his wound festered, his Greek comrades marooned him alone on the island of Lemnos, though he carried the bow of Heracles they would later need.
greek_mythology.explanation: The companions he had joined in a common cause abandoned him at the moment he most needed protection.
greek_mythology.tie_back: Philoctetes’ comrades are the Kural’s small-minded friends, who give no protection when it is due.
greek_mythology._accuracy_note: Good illustration of abandonment; summarised, and the play is about fellow soldiers rather than private friends.

philosophy.quote_or_event: Cicero has Laelius quote Ennius’s line that a sure friend is discerned in an unsure situation, and observes that many fail this test, deserting friends in adversity.
philosophy.explanation: For Cicero, adversity is the touchstone of friendship, and those who desert in hardship were never true friends.
philosophy.tie_back: The Kural applies the same touchstone and concludes that friends who fail it are better not had.
philosophy._accuracy_note: Close in substance; paraphrased because the translation could not be verified live.

kurals.tamil:
பேதை பெருங்கெழீஇ நட்பின் அறிவுடையார்
ஏதின்மை கோடி உறும்.
kurals.transliteration:
Pedhai perungezheei natpin arivudaiyaar
edhinmai kodi urum.
kurals.meaning: Being a stranger, or even an opponent, to wise people is worth ten million times more than the closest friendship with a fool.
kurals.elementary: If you’re building a sandcastle, a careful kid who doesn’t like you will still not knock it over, but a clumsy best friend might jump right on it while trying to help. Sometimes a sensible rival is safer than a silly friend.
kurals.university: The couplet sets pedhai perung kezheei natpu (பேதை பெருங்கெழீஇ நட்பு), ‘the greatly intimate friendship of a fool’, against arivudaiyaar edhinmai (அறிவுடையார் ஏதின்மை), and the reading of edhinmai divides commentators. Edhilaar means ‘strangers, outsiders’, and Mu. Varadarasanar and Puliyur Kesigan take edhinmai as ‘the absence of friendship’, being unconnected to the wise; Solomon Pappaiah and Kalaignar sharpen it to ‘enmity’ (பகை), giving the more striking proverb ‘a wise enemy is better than a foolish friend’. Kezheei (கெழீஇ) is the alapedai form of kezhu-, ‘to be closely joined’. ‘Kodi urum’ (கோடி உறும்) means ‘is worth a crore’, i.e., ten million times over. The texts agree; the sandhi-joined edition writes ‘நட்பி னறிவுடையா ரேதின்மை’.

hinduism.quote_or_event: In a Panchatantra story, a king appoints his pet monkey as bodyguard; when a fly settles on the sleeping king, the monkey swings a sword at it and kills the king, and the tale is set beside one in which a wise thief saves a life, to teach that a wise enemy is better than a foolish friend.
hinduism.explanation: The monkey’s devotion is real, but its foolishness makes its closeness deadly.
hinduism.tie_back: This is the Kural’s comparison in story form: the fool’s intimacy does more harm than the wise man’s enmity.
hinduism.source: Panchatantra, Book I (Mitrabheda), the king and the foolish monkey
hinduism._accuracy_note: Strong match; recensions differ in detail, so summarised rather than quoted.

christianity.quote_or_event: “He that walketh with wise men shall be wise: but a companion of fools shall be destroyed.”
christianity.explanation: Proverbs contrasts the gains of walking with the wise against the ruin that comes from keeping company with fools.
christianity.tie_back: Both texts judge friendship with fools as harmful and closeness to the wise as valuable.
christianity._accuracy_note: Very close; Proverbs lacks the idea that even the wise man’s distance is preferable.

islam.quote_or_event: “The example of a good pious companion and an evil one is that of a person carrying musk and another blowing a pair of bellows.”
islam.explanation: The Prophet compares a good companion to a perfume seller whose scent rubs off on you, and a bad one to a blacksmith whose bellows burn your clothes or leave a foul smell.
islam.tie_back: As in the Kural, simply being near the wrong person damages you, however close the bond.
islam._accuracy_note: Good match on the harm of bad company; contrasts good and evil rather than wise and foolish.

judaism.quote_or_event: King Rehoboam rejected the counsel of the elders who had served his father Solomon and followed the young men who had grown up with him; their advice to answer the people harshly led ten tribes to break away.
judaism.explanation: Rehoboam preferred the familiar intimacy of foolish peers to the counsel of the wise, and lost most of his kingdom.
judaism.tie_back: This is the Kural’s warning in history: a fool’s close friendship costs far more than distance from the wise.

buddhism.quote_or_event: “Better it is to live alone; there is no fellowship with a fool. Live alone and do no evil; be carefree like an elephant in the elephant forest.”
buddhism.explanation: The Dhammapada declares that there is no real companionship to be had with a fool.
buddhism.tie_back: Valluvar and the Buddha agree that a fool’s intimacy is worth less than none.
buddhism._accuracy_note: Near-direct match on refusing a fool’s fellowship; lacks the ‘wise enemy’ comparison.

greek_mythology.quote_or_event: In Aesop’s fable, a Mouse ‘formed an intimate acquaintance with a Frog’, who tied their feet together and dragged him into the pond, where the Mouse drowned and a Hawk carried off both.
greek_mythology.explanation: A tie of close friendship with a heedless partner brings death to one and ruin to both.
greek_mythology.tie_back: It dramatises the Kural’s perung kezheei natpu, the tightly bound friendship that destroys.
greek_mythology.source: Aesop, The Mouse, the Frog, and the Hawk (tr. G. F. Townsend)
greek_mythology._accuracy_note: Fits the dangerous intimacy, but the Frog is malicious rather than foolish and there is no wise rival.

philosophy.quote_or_event: La Fontaine’s fable of the Bear and the Garden-Lover ends with the moral that nothing is as dangerous as an ignorant friend and that a wise enemy would be better: the bear, guarding his sleeping friend, kills him with a paving stone while trying to swat a fly.
philosophy.explanation: The bear’s loyalty is sincere; its stupidity is what kills.
philosophy.tie_back: This is almost exactly the Kural’s proverb: a fool’s close friendship is worse than a wise man’s enmity.
philosophy.source: Jean de La Fontaine, Fables VIII.10, L’Ours et l’Amateur des jardins
philosophy._accuracy_note: Near one-to-one match (likely drawn from the Indian tradition); paraphrased because the French text could not be checked live.

kurals.tamil:
நகைவகைய ராகிய நட்பின் பகைவரால்
பத்தடுத்த கோடி உறும்.
kurals.transliteration:
Nakaivakaiya raakiya natpin pakaivaraal
paththaduththa kodi urum.
kurals.meaning: What comes to you from your enemies is worth a hundred million times more than the friendship of people who only laugh along with you.
kurals.elementary: A friend who just giggles at everything never tells you there’s spinach in your teeth. Even someone who doesn’t like you might point it out. Sometimes honest criticism helps more than easy laughter.
kurals.university: Nakaivakaiyar (நகைவகையர்) are ‘those of the laughing kind’: Mu. Varadarasanar adds ‘laughing outwardly without love within’, Kalaignar ‘those who laugh and talk as a performance’, and Puliyur Kesigan ‘those useful only for idle talk and merriment’. Against them stands what comes from pakaivar (பகைவர், ‘enemies’), worth paththaduththa kodi (பத்தடுத்த கோடி), ‘ten crore’ or a hundred million times more. The exaggeration escalates the kodi of 816. Commentators differ on what an enemy provides: most modern glosses say ‘benefit’, while Kalaignar paradoxically says even the suffering enemies cause is worth more, because it at least makes one alert. The wording agrees across ytamizh and thirukkural.net; the sandhi-joined edition writes ‘நட்பிற் பகைவராற்’.

hinduism.quote_or_event: “Of a rascal and a serpent, the serpent is the better of the two, for he strikes only at the time he is destined to kill, while the former at every step.”
hinduism.explanation: Chanakya prefers an open, predictable danger to the constant harm of a bad person close at hand.
hinduism.tie_back: Like the Kural, it ranks the obvious enemy above the false companion.
hinduism.source: Chanakya Niti 3.4 (Sri Chanakya Niti-sastra, English translation)
hinduism._accuracy_note: Shares the paradoxical ranking; Chanakya speaks of a rascal, not specifically a laughing friend.

christianity.quote_or_event: “Judas, betrayest thou the Son of man with a kiss?”
christianity.explanation: Judas leads the arresting crowd to Jesus and identifies him with a friendly kiss.
christianity.tie_back: The open enemies with swords were less treacherous than the friendly gesture; the Kural likewise ranks enemies above friendship that is all surface.
christianity._accuracy_note: Vivid illustration of friendly appearance hiding harm; the Kural’s ‘laughers’ are shallow rather than treacherous.

islam.quote_or_event: “The Religion is sincerity.” We said, “To whom?” He said “To Allah, to His Book, To His Messenger, and to the leaders of the Muslims and their masses.”
islam.explanation: The Prophet makes sincere goodwill, nasiha (often rendered sincere counsel), the core of religion in every relationship.
islam.tie_back: The Kural’s laughing friends offer the opposite of nasiha: pleasant noise without honest concern.
islam._accuracy_note: Next-best match: it sets the standard of sincerity but does not compare friends and enemies.

judaism.quote_or_event: “Faithful are the wounds of a friend; but the kisses of an enemy are deceitful.”
judaism.explanation: Proverbs holds that honest wounds from a true friend are worth more than an enemy’s pleasant kisses.
judaism.tie_back: Both texts value painful honesty over pleasant surface affection, though they assign the roles differently.
judaism._accuracy_note: Shared preference for honest hurt over pleasant falsity; Proverbs praises the friend’s rebuke, the Kural the enemy’s value.

buddhism.quote_or_event: “(iii) he tries to gain one’s favor by empty words”
buddhism.explanation: Among the marks of the ‘lip-service’ friend, a foe in the guise of a friend, the Buddha lists courting favour with empty talk.
buddhism.tie_back: This is the Kural’s nakaivakaiyar, whose friendship is laughter and talk with nothing inside.
buddhism._accuracy_note: Good match on hollow sociability; no comparison with enemies.

greek_mythology.quote_or_event: Diogenes Laertius reports that Antisthenes, the follower of Socrates, advised paying attention to one’s enemies, because they are the first to notice one’s mistakes.
greek_mythology.explanation: For Antisthenes an enemy’s hostile attention is a kind of free audit.
greek_mythology.tie_back: It gives a reason for the Kural’s paradox: an enemy’s scrutiny serves you better than friends who only laugh.
greek_mythology.source: Diogenes Laertius, Lives of Eminent Philosophers, Book 6 (Antisthenes)
greek_mythology._accuracy_note: Close in idea; Greek philosophical anecdote rather than myth, paraphrased and not verified live.

philosophy.quote_or_event: In his essay How to Profit by One’s Enemies, Plutarch argues that an enemy’s constant watchfulness keeps a person careful and self-correcting in ways that indulgent friends do not.
philosophy.explanation: Plutarch turns enmity into a moral tool: those who hunt for your faults make you guard against them.
philosophy.tie_back: This explains why Valluvar says enemies yield far more than friends who only share a laugh.
philosophy.source: Plutarch, Moralia, How to Profit by One’s Enemies

kurals.tamil:
ஒல்லும் கருமம் உடற்று பவர்கேண்மை
சொல்லாடார் சோர விடல்.
kurals.transliteration:
Ollum karumam udatru pavarkenmai
sollaadaar sora vidal.
kurals.meaning: With those who spoil a task that could easily be done, pretending they cannot help, let the friendship quietly slacken without making an announcement of it.
kurals.elementary: If a friend always says ‘I can’t’ whenever you need a small hand, even when they easily could, you don’t need to have a big fight. You can just slowly spend more time with friends who do help.
kurals.university: Ollum karumam (ஒல்லும் கருமம்) is ‘a task that can be done’; udatrupavar (உடற்றுபவர்) are those who ‘harass’ or ruin it, which Solomon Pappaiah and the classical English versions read as feigning inability to do what they could, and Mu. Varadarasanar and Kalaignar as making the possible impossible. The remedy is notably mild: sollaadaar (சொல்லாடார்), ‘without speaking of it’, sora vidal (சோர விடல்), ‘let it slacken’. Mu. Varadarasanar and Kalaignar read sollaadaar as ‘without letting them know’, Puliyur Kesigan as ‘by ceasing to talk with them’. The counsel is gradual disengagement rather than confrontation, a tactful way to avoid making a fresh enemy. The texts agree; the sandhi-joined edition writes ‘ஒல்லுங் கரும முடற்று பவர்கேண்மை’.

hinduism.quote_or_event: In the Mahabharata, Shalya agrees to serve as Karna’s charioteer at Kurukshetra but, having privately promised Yudhishthira to weaken Karna, belittles him throughout the battle and undermines his morale.
hinduism.explanation: The man whose job was to carry Karna’s chariot to victory uses his position to spoil the very task he was given.
hinduism.tie_back: Shalya is the Kural’s udatrupavar, the companion who ruins a doable task from the inside.
hinduism.source: Mahabharata, Udyoga Parva and Karna Parva (Shalya as Karna’s charioteer)
hinduism._accuracy_note: Strong illustration of sabotage by an ally; summarised, and it lacks the advice to withdraw quietly.

christianity.quote_or_event: “And one of you say unto them, Depart in peace, be ye warmed and filled; notwithstanding ye give them not those things which are needful to the body; what doth it profit?”
christianity.explanation: James mocks those who offer warm words to someone in need while doing nothing they could easily do.
christianity.tie_back: This is the Kural’s friend who could help but finds a way not to.
christianity._accuracy_note: Good match on withholding easy help; no counsel about quietly ending the friendship.

islam.quote_or_event: “And they will swear by Allah, ‘If we were able, we would have gone forth with you,’ destroying themselves [through false oaths], and Allah knows that indeed they are liars.”
islam.explanation: The hypocrites excuse themselves from the expedition by claiming they were unable, when in truth they did not want the hardship.
islam.tie_back: This is exactly the Kural’s pretended inability over a task that could be done.
islam._accuracy_note: Very close on feigned inability; the setting is a military campaign, and no quiet withdrawal is advised.

judaism.quote_or_event: “Withhold not good from them to whom it is due, when it is in the power of thine hand to do it. Say not unto thy neighbour, Go, and come again, and to morrow I will give; when thou hast it by thee.”
judaism.explanation: Proverbs forbids putting off a neighbour with excuses when one is perfectly able to help now.
judaism.tie_back: The Kural describes the friend who does exactly this; Proverbs names it as a fault.
judaism._accuracy_note: Close on the fault; addresses the would-be helper rather than his friend.

buddhism.quote_or_event: “(iv) when opportunity for service has arisen, he expresses his inability.”
buddhism.explanation: The Buddha lists this as a mark of the ‘lip-service’ friend, a foe in the guise of a friend.
buddhism.tie_back: This is the Kural’s udatrupavar almost word for word: the friend who pleads inability when the chance to help arrives.
buddhism._accuracy_note: Near one-to-one match on feigned inability.

greek_mythology.quote_or_event: When the Greek leaders came to recruit Odysseus for the war against Troy, he pretended to be mad, ploughing a field with an ill-matched team; Palamedes exposed him by placing the infant Telemachus in the plough’s path.
greek_mythology.explanation: Odysseus feigned incapacity to escape a duty he was fully able to perform.
greek_mythology.tie_back: It is the Kural’s pretended inability in mythic form.
greek_mythology._accuracy_note: Clear case of feigned inability; Odysseus is not a false friend in the Kural’s sense, and the passage is summarised.

philosophy.quote_or_event: Cicero has Laelius endorse Cato’s advice that friendships which have gone wrong should be unstitched gradually rather than torn apart, unless some intolerable wrong makes an immediate break unavoidable.
philosophy.explanation: Cicero prefers a gradual, quiet loosening to a public rupture that might turn a friend into an enemy.
philosophy.tie_back: This matches the Kural’s sollaadaar sora vidal, let it slacken without speaking of it, very closely.
philosophy._accuracy_note: Very close on the method of ending; paraphrased because the translation could not be verified live.

kurals.tamil:
கனவினும் இன்னாது மன்னோ வினைவேறு
சொல்வேறு பட்டார் தொடர்பு.
kurals.transliteration:
Kanavinum innaadhu manno vinaiveru
solveru pattaar thodarpu.
kurals.meaning: Friendship with people whose deeds are one thing and whose words another is painful even in a dream.
kurals.elementary: If a friend promises to save you a seat and then gives it to someone else, and does it again and again, you start feeling uneasy even when you’re just thinking about them. A friend’s words and actions should match.
kurals.university: The couplet names the fault precisely: vinai veru, sol veru (வினை வேறு, சொல் வேறு), ‘deed apart, word apart’, the divorce of action from speech. Kanavinum (கனவினும், ‘even in a dream’) intensifies: such a connection hurts not only in waking life, as Puliyur Kesigan spells out, but even in sleep. Manno (மன்னோ) is an emotive particle of emphasis or lament, which Sivayogi Sivakumar renders as a rhetorical question, ‘will it not give pain even in a dream?’ The word here is thodarpu (தொடர்பு, ‘connection, association’) rather than natpu, perhaps suggesting such people never achieve true friendship. All three texts agree; the sandhi-joined edition prints ‘கனவினு மின்னாது’.

hinduism.quote_or_event: In the Mahabharata, Duryodhana’s side invites the Pandavas to Varanavata with gracious words and builds them a fine house there, secretly made of lac and other flammable materials so that it can be set on fire while they sleep.
hinduism.explanation: The gracious invitation and the deadly intent are the starkest split between word and deed in the epic.
hinduism.tie_back: This is the Kural’s vinai veru, sol veru, and a reason such ties haunt even one’s dreams.
hinduism.source: Mahabharata, Adi Parva (the house of lac, Jatugriha)
hinduism._accuracy_note: Clear illustration of words contradicting deeds; it involves open rivals rather than friends, and is summarised.

christianity.quote_or_event: “My little children, let us not love in word, neither in tongue; but in deed and in truth.”
christianity.explanation: John insists that love must be shown in action, not only spoken.
christianity.tie_back: This is the positive form of the Kural’s complaint against those whose words and deeds diverge.
christianity._accuracy_note: Direct match on the word-and-deed principle; phrased as an exhortation rather than a warning.

islam.quote_or_event: “O you who have believed, why do you say what you do not do? Great is hatred in the sight of Allah that you say what you do not do.”
islam.explanation: The Qur’an condemns the gap between what people say and what they actually do.
islam.tie_back: The Kural’s vinai veru, sol veru is exactly the fault these verses denounce.
islam._accuracy_note: Near one-to-one match on the word-deed split.

judaism.quote_or_event: “The words of his mouth were smoother than butter, but war was in his heart: his words were softer than oil, yet were they drawn swords.”
judaism.explanation: The psalmist describes a former companion whose gentle speech covered hostile intent.
judaism.tie_back: It is the Kural’s split between word and deed, and the anguish of the psalm matches ‘painful even in a dream’.
judaism._accuracy_note: Strong match on soft words and hostile deeds.

buddhism.quote_or_event: “(i) he makes friendly profession as regards the past, (ii) he makes friendly profession as regards the future, (iii) he tries to gain one’s favor by empty words, (iv) when opportunity for service has arisen, he expresses his inability.”
buddhism.explanation: The ‘lip-service’ friend is all professions of goodwill about past and future, with nothing done now.
buddhism.tie_back: This is the Kural’s friend whose words go one way and deeds another.
buddhism._accuracy_note: Close match on profession without performance.

greek_mythology.quote_or_event: In the Iliad, Achilles tells the embassy sent by Agamemnon that he hates like the gates of Hades the man who hides one thing in his heart and says another.
greek_mythology.explanation: Achilles names the gap between inner intent and outward speech as the thing he most despises.
greek_mythology.tie_back: Achilles’ loathing echoes the Kural’s judgment that such people are a torment even in dreams.
greek_mythology._accuracy_note: Close match on duplicity; paraphrased because the translation could not be verified live.

philosophy.quote_or_event: “… when he has been deceived by the pretences of the other person, it is just that he should complain against his deceiver; he will complain with more justice than one does against people who counterfeit the currency, inasmuch as the wrongdoing is concerned with something more valuable.”
philosophy.explanation: Aristotle says the bitterest complaints between friends arise when one pretended to love the other for his character while really loving him for profit or pleasure, and he ranks this deception above counterfeiting money.
philosophy.tie_back: Aristotle, like the Kural, treats a friendship in which outward profession differs from the real disposition as a grievous wrong.
philosophy.source: Aristotle, Nicomachean Ethics, IX.3, 1165b (tr. W. D. Ross)
philosophy._accuracy_note: Verified verbatim on the MIT Internet Classics Archive (Ross). Strong match on the wrong of a friend whose show differs from his reality. Aristotle contrasts pretended and real motives rather than words and deeds, and the Kural's image of the pain reaching even into dreams is absent.

kurals.tamil:
எனைத்தும் குறுகுதல் ஓம்பல் மனைக்கெழீஇ
மன்றில் பழிப்பார் தொடர்பு.
kurals.transliteration:
Enaiththum kurukudhal ombal manaikkezheei
mandril pazhippaar thodarpu.
kurals.meaning: Guard against coming even slightly close to people who are friendly with you at home but run you down in public.
kurals.elementary: Imagine someone who plays nicely with you at your house but makes fun of you in front of the whole class. That’s not a real friend, and it’s wise to keep your distance from them.
kurals.university: The chapter closes on the double-faced friend: manaik kezheei (மனைக் கெழீஇ), ‘intimate in the house’, and mandril pazhippaar (மன்றில் பழிப்பார்), ‘those who revile in the manram’, the public hall or assembly where reputations are made. The prescription is the strongest in the chapter: enaiththum kurukudhal ombal (எனைத்தும் குறுகுதல் ஓம்பல்), ‘guard against approaching in any measure at all’. Where 811 and 818 allowed a gradual waning, here even the slightest contact is to be avoided, since such a person turns private trust into public damage. Mu. Varadarasanar, Solomon Pappaiah and Puliyur Kesigan all read manai literally as ‘home’, while Kalaignar’s gloss refers to private moments. The texts agree; the sandhi-joined edition writes ‘எனைத்துங் குறுகுத லோம்பன்’ and ‘மன்றிற் பழிப்பார்’.

hinduism.quote_or_event: “Avoid him who talks sweetly before you but tries to ruin you behind your back, for he is like a pitcher of poison with milk on top.”
hinduism.explanation: Chanakya warns against the person who is sweet in your presence and destructive in your absence.
hinduism.tie_back: This is the Kural’s home-friend and public slanderer, and both texts prescribe avoidance.
hinduism.source: Chanakya Niti 2.5 (Sri Chanakya Niti-sastra, English translation)
hinduism._accuracy_note: Very close match in both diagnosis and remedy.

christianity.quote_or_event: “I speak not of you all: I know whom I have chosen: but that the scripture may be fulfilled, He that eateth bread with me hath lifted up his heel against me.”
christianity.explanation: At the Last Supper Jesus applies Psalm 41:9 to Judas, the table companion who will betray him.
christianity.tie_back: Sharing bread at home and turning on someone outside is the pattern the Kural tells us to avoid.
christianity._accuracy_note: Strong match on intimacy at the table turned to betrayal; the harm is betrayal rather than public slander.

islam.quote_or_event: “The worst people in the Sight of Allah on the Day of Resurrection will be the double faced people who appear to some people with one face and to other people with another face.”
islam.explanation: The Prophet names the two-faced person, who shows different faces in different company, as among the worst of people.
islam.tie_back: The Kural’s friend at home and slanderer in the assembly is exactly this double-faced person.

judaism.quote_or_event: “For it was not an enemy that reproached me; then I could have borne it … But it was thou, a man mine equal, my guide, and mine acquaintance. We took sweet counsel together, and walked unto the house of God in company.”
judaism.explanation: The psalmist says he could have endured an enemy’s reproach, but the one shaming him is a close companion who once shared his confidence.
judaism.tie_back: This is the pain of the Kural’s friend who is intimate in private and reviles in public.
judaism._accuracy_note: Very close emotionally; the psalm laments rather than prescribes avoidance.

buddhism.quote_or_event: “(i) he approves of his friend’s evil deeds, (ii) he disapproves his friend’s good deeds, (iii) he praises him in his presence, (iv) he speaks ill of him in his absence.”
buddhism.explanation: The Buddha describes the flatterer, a foe in the guise of a friend, as one who praises to your face and disparages you behind your back.
buddhism.tie_back: Items (iii) and (iv) are the Kural’s couplet almost exactly, and the Sutta’s remedy, to avoid such people from afar, matches its counsel.

greek_mythology.quote_or_event: In one strand of the myth (Euripides’ Orestes; Diodorus Siculus 4.74), Tantalus, honoured as a guest at the gods’ own table, repaid their intimacy by blurting their secrets to mortals, and was punished eternally.
greek_mythology.explanation: Tantalus turned the privileges of private friendship into public exposure of his hosts.
greek_mythology.tie_back: He fits the Kural’s pattern of intimacy at home turned against the host in public.
greek_mythology.source: Euripides, Orestes; Diodorus Siculus, Library of History 4.74
greek_mythology._accuracy_note: Next-best match: the myth has several versions of Tantalus’s crime, and his offence is indiscretion rather than slander.

philosophy.quote_or_event: “The dissembler is a man, for instance, who accosts his enemies and engages readily in talk with them, to show that he bears no grudge, and who praises to their faces the very men he slanders behind their backs …”
philosophy.explanation: In the first of his character sketches, Theophrastus describes the dissembler, who is friendly in private encounters while running the same people down elsewhere.
philosophy.tie_back: This is almost exactly the person the Kural warns against: friendly in private and disparaging in public.
philosophy.source: Theophrastus, Characters, I (The Dissembler) (tr. Charles E. Bennett and William A. Hammond)
philosophy._accuracy_note: Verified verbatim in the Bennett and Hammond translation (1902) on Project Gutenberg (eBook #58242). Near one-to-one description of the type; Theophrastus describes the character but, unlike the Kural, gives no explicit command to avoid him.
